dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?

Yes, hello. My name is Timothy Almy. I'm putting up a fence and I wanted to find out about the rules. I called the main number first and the woman there said, call Zoning, and then I said, well, is that a different office, and she said yes. So here I am.
Okay, you're in the right place, Mr. Almy. So you're planning a fence. Is this at your own home?
Yes, I'm the homeowner. I own the house outright. It's a corner lot, so I've got street on two sides.
Got it. A corner lot does matter, so I'm glad you mentioned it. What kind of fence are you thinking about?
Pressure-treated wood, six feet tall. Dog-eared pickets, the guy said, or flat top, I haven't decided. But six feet. He said that's what most people get, and I said, well, that's what I want.
Okay. And is that along the back of the yard, or would it run along either street side?

Well, that's my question, really. It would run along the side street, and then across the back. So I wondered whether the sight lines matter. For the cars at the corner. I don't know if that's a thing.

It is a thing, yes. On a corner, the city looks at whether a fence blocks drivers' view of the intersection. Generally, a tall solid fence close to the corner is the sort of thing that gets looked at closely.
I figured. My neighbor across the way had a hedge, and somebody said it had to come down, and I said, was that the city, and he said he thought so. I don't know.
I can't speak to that hedge, but it's the same idea. So, what's your actual question on the permit?

Do I need to pull a permit before the guy starts? He's got a crew coming, he said he could start the week after next. And I said, well, do you pull the permit, and he said some people do it themselves, so I thought I'd better ask.

In general, yes, a fence usually needs a permit here, and it should be in place before any work begins. Sometimes the contractor handles the application, sometimes the owner does. You'll want to settle that with him in writing so nobody assumes.
All right. So I'd need it before he digs the first hole.
Correct, before any posts go in. We'd also want a simple drawing of your lot showing where the fence goes. A survey or plot plan helps if you have one.
I think I have a plot plan from when I bought the place. It's in a folder somewhere. Would that work?
That's often a good start. Does it show the property lines and where the house sits?
Yes, it has the house drawn in, and the lines with the measurements. It's pretty old, but nothing has been changed.

And the other thing. How close to the property line is allowed? I told the guy, I want it right on the line, and he said, you might need to set it in a little. I said, how much, and he said ask the city.

Right, so that's a fair question. The setback depends on your zoning district and, on a corner lot, which side is considered the front. I don't want to give you a number that's wrong for your lot. If you give me your address, I can look up the district and have someone confirm it.
Oh, I'd rather not give the address over the phone right now. Can I just come in with the plot plan?
Sure, that works fine. Bring the plot plan, and a sketch showing the fence location and the height. Staff at the counter can go over the setbacks and the corner sight area with you.
What are the hours? I was going to come Wednesday, but they have a half day at school that day, and that threw off my plans. I'm picking up my grandson, so I'm tied up in the afternoon.
We're open weekdays during regular business hours, so a morning visit Wednesday would be fine. If mornings are better, I'd suggest coming in before noon.
Morning, okay. I'll do that. So to sum up, I need a permit before the work, bring the plot plan, and they'll tell me the distance from the line and the corner thing.
That's it. And tell your contractor to hold off on starting until the permit's issued.
I will. I'll say, the city said wait, and he'll have to wait. Thank you, Anita.
You're welcome, Mr. Almy. Have a good weekend.
You too. Goodbye.
